# Lomasakaṅgiyabhaddekaratta Sutta (MN 134 (PTS MN iii 199))
**ID:** MN 134 (PTS MN iii 199)

**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Lomasakaṅgiyabhaddekaratta Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Lomasakaṅgiya and One Fine Night

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Lomasakaṅgiyabhaddekaratta Sutta* (MN 134) is the fourth discourse in the *Bhaddekaratta* cycle of the *Majjhimanikāya* (MN 131–134), which centers on a poem and exposition (*uddesa* and *vibhaṅga*) urging strenuous insight into present phenomena rather than clinging to the past or future [von Hinüber 1996; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Emmrich 2012]. The sutta begins at the Nigrodhārāma in Kapilavatthu, where the deity Candana visits the monk Lomasakaṅgiya and asks whether he knows the summary and exposition of the *Bhaddekaratta* [Holz 2012; Skilling 2008]. When Lomasakaṅgiya admits that he does not, Candana recites the verses, explaining that he had previously heard the Buddha preach them while residing among the Tāvatiṃsa devas at the foot of the Paricchattaka tree on the Paṇḍukambala stone slab [Skilling 2008; Holz 2012]. Encouraged to master the verses, Lomasakaṅgiya travels to Sāvatthī to request the full teaching directly from the Buddha, who delivers the poem and its detailed analysis [SuttaCentral; Humphreys 1956; Holz 2012].
In its commentary (*Papañcasūdanī*), the text is contextualized within the Buddha's seventh year after awakening, assigning this heavenly sermon to the same sojourn as his teaching of the Abhidhamma [Anālayo 2014]. The commentary also uses the dialogue on learning the discourse to distinguish degrees of textual retention: listening silently (*uggaṇhāti*), vocal rehearsal (*pariyāpuṇāti*), and teaching others (*dhāreti*) [Drewes 2015].
Both SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus align MN 134 closely with its sister suttas in the *Majjhimanikāya* (MN 131, MN 132, and especially MN 133), as well as the *Mūgapakkhajātaka* (Ja 538), the *Lomasakaṅgiyatthera-apadāna* (Tha-Ap 550), and the *Nettippakaraṇa* (*Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*, Ne 37) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Holz 2012]. External parallels include two Chinese translations—*Madhyama-āgama* 166 (MĀ 166 / T 26) and the standalone *Zunshang jing* 尊上經 (T 77)—as well as Sanskrit fragments in the *Sagāthāvarga* and Tibetan versions of the *Bhadrakarātrī-sūtra* (D 313) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Holz 2012]. In the Chinese counterparts, however, the specific narrative reference to the Buddha preaching in Tāvatiṃsa is absent [Skilling 2008].
